text.p: A long-awaited report on governance of British companies on Tuesday said that companies and shareholders should be flexible when it comes to working out how a company should perform.

The report by the Hampel committee, headed by ICI chairman Sir Ronald Hampel, came out against "box-ticking" -- where companies have to comply with lists of principles -- and also concluded recommendations should not distinguish between small and large companies.

"Box-ticking is neither fair to companies, nor likely to be efficient in preventing abuse," the committee said in its preliminary report, which was immediately welcomed by the Institute of Directors (IoD), an association of company bosses.

The Hampel report, which follows the earlier Cadbury code on governance and Greenbury recommendations on executive pay, said firms and shareholders should apply broad principles of governance, "flexibly, with common sense, and with due regard to companies' individual circumstances."
The report recommended companies should include in the annual report a narrative account of how they apply the broad principles set out in detail.

Hampel said executive and non-executive directors should continue to have the same duties under the law, and for a board to be effective, it was essential that management provided it with appropriate and timely information.
It said there was overwhelming support in the UK to stick with the system of one board of directors and virtually none for a two-tier board involving supervisory directors.

The report also recommended flexibility over the Cadbury recommendation that the roles of chairman and chief executive, although it said separation was to be preferred and combination should be justified.
"We do not consider that separation of the roles of chariman and chief executive should be a firm rule, and that in a number of companies, the combination of the roles can be justified," Hampel said.
It also called for a lead non-executive director to be identified in the annual report, regardless of whether the roles of chairman and chief executive were combined.

On renumeration, a controversial issue in recent years with some "fat cat" directors accused of excessive pay, Hampel said, "We do not recommend further refinement in the Greenbury code provisions relating to performance-related pay." The report urged renumeration committees to use their judgement on performance schemes. "Total rewards from such schemes should not be excessive," it said.
The report saw no objection to paying non-executives in company shares, but did not recommend it as a universal practice.
On institutional shareholder responsibility, the report said, "We recommend pension fund trustees to encourage fund managers to take a long view in managing their investments."

It stopped short of recommending that voting at meetings should be compulsory, but said institutional investors had an obligation to their clients to "adopt a considered policy on voting their shares."

Hampel also suggested shareholder bodies the Association of British Insurers and National Association of Pension Funds should examine a problem caused by the existence of different and incompatible shareholder voting guidelines.
The committee said directors should be given appropriate instruction when first appointed to a board and subsequently as necessary.
The majority of directors should be independent and this applies to all companies, it added.

IoD director general Tim Melville-Ross said in a statement, "The Hampel Committee have produced an eminently sensible report, which emphasises that corporate governance is about enterprise and prosperity, as well as accountability."
Hampel invited comments on the report to arrive by the end of September, with the aim of producing a final report with a single set of recommendations uniting Cadbury and Greenbury, in December.
